_: MEASURED LIFT PER NAMED STRUCTURE. This file is the ONLY authority on what a structure has been measured to do; `base_catalog.Structure` deliberately carries no lift field, so the catalog can never disagree with the harness. `published: false` means we have no number -- either it was never measured or it was measured and refused -- and `base_catalog.meta()` surfaces None for both, because to a member they say the same honest thing. The reasons stay here for anyone auditing.
method: Lift = conditional rate - pattern-free rate, where the pattern-free half is restricted to the YEARS the structure actually fired in (the baseline drifts: target-first ran 17.1% in 2018 and 35.7% in 2020). Anchors are stepped by the full 20-session horizon so no two observations share a forward window. The CI is a 400-draw CLUSTER BOOTSTRAP resampling tickers with replacement, because detections cluster by ticker and a two-proportion SE assumes that away. The null re-runs the IDENTICAL detector over MOVING-BLOCK resampled series (21-bar blocks) so local volatility clustering survives and only the long-range order is destroyed -- an iid shuffle would hand a quiet-regime detector a free volatility premium.
gates: FOUR gates, and all must pass or NO number is published. (0) THE LIFT MUST BE POSITIVE. This gate was missing and it FIRED: `cheat-3c` measured -1.10pp with a CI of [-2.16, -0.09] against a null max of -3.91pp and published, because its interval excludes zero (both bounds negative) and its lower bound clears a null that is even more negative. A structure that reliably UNDERPERFORMS its own baseline was surfaced to members as a measured edge. A negative result is a finding and stays here with its reasons; it is not a lift to put in front of anyone. (1) The lift's 95% CI excludes zero. (2) The CI's LOWER BOUND exceeds the random-data null's maximum -- not the point estimate, which let a +32.97pp lift on n=13 through on the first run. (3) n is whatever (1) requires, derived rather than typed. AND A PUBLISHED ROW MUST CARRY 30 NULL TRIALS, not the 5 used to screen: the null's maximum can only grow with more draws, so a small trial count is a strictly easier gate and would be a dial pointing at publication. The escalation has changed a verdict in BOTH directions -- stage-4-breakdown passed at 30 after failing at 5 on a narrower sample, and buyable-gap-up failed at 30 after passing at 5.
sample: Seeded-random draw from the screener universe, up to 3,000 daily bars per ticker. The size differs per structure and per run, so it is recorded on each row as `sample_tickers` rather than claimed once here; a row's window is `tools/run_lift_ledger.py::WINDOWS[key]`.
baseline_metric: P(+10% before -8% within 20 sessions). Measured unconditionally over the whole 3,705-name universe by an independent code path: 27.51% target-first, 33.41% stop-first, 39.08% neither. The per-structure pattern-free baselines below came out at 27.01-28.71%, which is the cross-check that this harness measures what it claims to.
limitations:
⚠️ A PREDICTION IN THIS FIELD WAS FALSIFIED BY THE DATA, and the correction matters more than the original claim. It read: 'widening the sample can tighten an estimate but not flip its sign.' The full-universe re-measure flipped two. `cup-with-handle` went from -7.18pp on 279 tickers -- where I wrote a confident note explaining why the most famous base in the industry sat below its own null -- to -0.18pp with an interval straddling zero on 3,408: a NON-EVENT, and the small-sample negative was noise. `square-box` went the other way, from an interval straddling zero to a published +0.99pp. Sign stability under resampling is not something a narrow sample entitles you to assume.

(1) SAMPLE -- now the full universe. Every row was re-measured on 3,456 tickers (those carrying enough history for its window), not the 279 the first pass used. Each row still records its own `sample_tickers`, since the usable count differs by window. This was run ONCE and its output stands, including for structures that came back worse; re-running at successively wider samples until a structure passes would be p-hacking with extra steps.

(2) NULL DEPTH -- `null_trials` is part of every verdict, not a footnote to it. A row refused at 5 trials was refused by a null that could only get WEAKER with fewer draws, so its refusal is safe. A row PUBLISHED at fewer than 30 is not, which is why every published row carries 30 and a rail enforces it.

(3) DIRECTION -- the metric is P(+10% before -8%), a LONG outcome, and it is applied to every structure regardless of bias. For a BEARISH structure a positive lift therefore says price resolved UPWARD more often than baseline, which is an oversold-bounce reading rather than confirmation the structure works. `stage-4-breakdown` publishes +7.30pp under exactly that reading. The number is real; the interpretation is not the obvious one, and a directional metric per bias is the honest next step.

(4) IMPLEMENTATION SUBSETS -- several detectors are explicitly narrower than the rule they name, and each says so on its criteria: the buyable gap-up omits a volume gate whose two published phrasings differ by a factor of 1.67; the pocket pivot omits a fundamentals gate that is not computable from bars; the saucer is measured on daily bars although its house says the pattern is 'only visible on a weekly or monthly chart'. A gate not applied is a rejection not made, so those rows include names the full rule would refuse.

DATA HYGIENE, TESTED 2026-08-31 AND NOT SUPPORTED. An adversarial review raised a specific, serious hypothesis: `run_lift_ledger.load_universe` reads bars RAW -- no split repair, no listing cutoff, no bad-wick clamp -- while `outcome` is a bare threshold test on highs and lows. An unrepaired split leaves a fake ~50% down-cliff, which on the SHORT metric is a false WIN; splits follow large run-ups, and climax-top and parabolic-extension detect large run-ups. The prediction was therefore specific: the two SHORT rows should be inflated by cliff-carrying windows and the two LONG rows should not. MEASURED over 837 tickers by finding every >30% single-day close move and looking BACKWARD for a structure firing in the window that would grade it, the asymmetry is REVERSED. Win rate inside a cliff window minus the row's own published conditional rate: parabolic-extension (short) -8.5pp, climax-top (short) +4.9pp, darvas-box (long) +4.0pp, square-box (long) +8.0pp. The largest elevation is on a LONG row and the largest short row is DEPRESSED -- the opposite of what contamination would produce. Two further facts point the same way: most cliffs landing in these windows are UP (444 of 591 for parabolic-extension), and an up-cliff on a short metric is a LOSS; and 40.6% of tickers carry a >30% day at all, with the largest down-moves being identifiable real events (TYG and CHEF both on 2020-03-18, the COVID crash; SRPT's biotech collapses) rather than data defects. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SAY: it does not prove the store holds no unrepaired splits, and routing the harness through `bars_sanitize` the way `screener_backtest` does remains correct hygiene. It says the two published short rows do not rest on that contamination. NOTE FOR ANYONE RE-RUNNING THIS: `bars_sanitize` is INERT on the owner's machine -- every corporate-action fetch fails (rate limit / transport / missing FMP_API_KEY) and it returns its input unchanged, so a raw-versus-sanitised comparison there compares identical bars and measures nothing. That was this investigation's first dead end.

darvas-box.note:
+7.35pp, CI [+6.78pp, +7.96pp] at n=24,428, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached +1.10pp.

The first structure to publish and the only one that has now cleared the bar on two independent samples. A 1960s box-range rule outscoring every modern base in this library is not the result anyone expected, and it is worth saying why it is credible: the moving-block null was built specifically to strip out the volatility premium a box detector would earn by selecting quiet stretches, and it removed almost nothing. ⛔ The structure ALSO carries our own recency bound: without it the label matched 96.7% of the universe, because over 400 bars nearly every stock frames a box at some point. The published number belongs to the gated definition, not to 'a Darvas box existed here once'.

double-bottom.note:
+3.18pp, CI [+2.51pp, +3.82pp] at n=22,024, against a 5-trial null whose maximum reached +4.31pp.

⭐ THE CLEAREST CASE IN THE LEDGER FOR WHY THE NULL EXISTS. A positive result whose interval excludes zero, on 22,024 observations -- every screener in the industry would publish it. It is refused because the IDENTICAL detector on moving-block resampled series reaches a HIGHER number than the pessimistic end of the real one. Which is obvious once said: a W is two lows with a high between them, and noise makes those constantly. Widening the sample 12x did not rescue it; it confirmed it.

square-box.note:
+0.99pp, CI [+0.35pp, +1.58pp] at n=33,851, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached -0.81pp.

The smallest published edge in the ledger, and it flipped on evidence: at 279 tickers it was +1.07pp with a CI straddling zero and I wrote it up as a clean null result. At 3,456 tickers the interval excludes zero. ⛔ Its detector needed two corrections before it measured this at all -- the published rules alone matched 46.7% of the universe, and the tilt test that fixes that had to become a RATIO (drift over the box's own depth) because an absolute bound is scale-dependent: 10% of price across a 4-7 week box is a trend, across a 52-week base it is flat. A near-zero null is what makes this small number trustworthy: unlike the double bottom, whose detector finds +4.31pp on pure noise, this one has almost no mechanical edge on random data.

reasons: the lift's CI lower bound +0.1099 does not exceed the random-data null (max of 30 trials = +0.1140) at n=5374
buyable-gap-up.note:
+12.56pp, CI [+10.99, +13.93] at n=5,374, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached +11.40pp.

⭐ THE ESCALATION RULE WORKING IN THE OTHER DIRECTION. This PASSED its 5-trial screen -- a +12.56pp lift with a CI lower bound of +10.99pp against a null max of +10.42pp -- and FAILED the 30-trial escalation, because the null's upper tail kept climbing: +10.42pp on five draws, +11.40pp on thirty. That is precisely why the escalation runs in one direction only. Stage 4 moved the other way on a wider SAMPLE; this one moved back on a harder NULL, and both are the same discipline.

⚠️ Read the number with its known bias. The detector is an explicit SUBSET of the authors' rule -- their volume gate is not implemented, because it reaches us in two phrasings that differ by a factor of 1.67 and the research note says not to choose between them. A gate we do not apply is a gate whose rejections we do not make, so this measurement includes gap-ups the full rule would refuse.

-1.10pp, CI [-2.16pp, -0.09pp] at n=6,139, against a 5-trial null whose maximum reached -3.91pp.

⛔⛔ THE ROW THAT EXPOSED A HOLE IN THE GATE. It PUBLISHED with a NEGATIVE lift, because its interval excludes zero (both bounds negative) and its lower bound clears a null that is even more negative. The gate had never checked the sign, and the defect stayed invisible for as long as no structure happened to land in that position. Gate zero now requires a positive lift. The result itself stands as a finding: the best-sourced structure in the build -- nine criteria at high confidence -- does not beat its own baseline.

low-cheat.note:
+2.80pp, CI [+0.83, +4.56] at n=2,856, against a 5-trial null whose maximum reached -0.86pp.

⛔ REFUSED FOR A REASON THAT IS ABOUT PROCESS, NOT THE MARKET: it has only been SCREENED. It cleared the 5-trial screen comfortably -- the interval excludes zero and its lower bound sits well above a negative null -- and a published row requires 30 trials, because the gate compares against the null's MAXIMUM and a maximum can only grow with more draws. Its escalation is running and may take it either way: the buyable gap-up passed the same screen at +12.56pp and FAILED at 30 when its null climbed from +10.42pp to +11.40pp.

⚠️ Read it with its known gap. Minervini intends the low cheat for "larger cap names" and publishes NO cap floor -- a third party's ">$10B" is theirs, not his -- so this detector filters by size not at all and fires on small caps he would never apply it to. That biases the measurement, not merely the label.
